column1: Bren/s0|What did you do with the copy?|I told my neighbour I had not checked the story and asked them not to pass it on as fact.|Was Elowen angry?|She wanted an answer, not an apology impressive enough to replace one.

Bren/s1|What if no witness survives?|I record the source and say what I cannot verify.|Can a witness remember wrongly?|Certainly. A name gives me someone to question, not permission to stop questioning.

Bren/e0|Why not write the answer beside it?|I do. Leaving room reminds me that the first answer may be incomplete.|Do you keep your old questions?|Yes. They show me why I believed something at the time.
Bren/e1|What changes in the telling?|Details, motives, sometimes who was even there.|Can comparing versions help?|Yes, particularly when I can trace where each teller heard it.

Bren/w0|What made the page look reliable?|A formal heading and confident language. Neither told me whether its writer was honest.|Did anyone correct you?|Elowen asked questions I could not answer. That was more useful than agreeing with the page.|Why be embarrassed to admit it?|Because I had sounded so certain when I repeated it.

Bren/w1|How will you send corrections?|To the people I gave copies to, with the reasons the account was unreliable.|What if they already passed it on?|I will ask them to pass the correction on too.|Will you stop copying stories?|No. I will make the source and any uncertainty clear.

Berta/s0|What questions did she ask?|Why two similar plants needed different preparation. Sensible questions that required careful answers.|Did teaching tire you out?|It did, but repeating a method without understanding it would have worried me more.
Berta/s1|Do you miss running the stall?|The regular customers, chiefly. I do not miss every early start.|Does Wren welcome your visits?|When I remember it is her work now and stop rearranging it.

Berta/e0|Was the wrong label dangerous?|It could have confused the preparations. We checked the contents before anything was sold.|Did you thank Wren?|Yes. My pride was less important than a correct label.
Berta/e1|Do you go back to sleep?|Rarely. I enjoy an early morning more when nobody is waiting for me to open.|Do you still visit customers?|As neighbours. Being retired need not mean disappearing.

Berta/w0|Why would someone hide an injury?|They may fear questions about where it happened, or be unable to spare the cost of care.|What happens when they wait?|An injury can worsen. Then the treatment and lost work cost them more.|Can a healer help with the fear?|By listening and treating people without turning every visit into an interrogation.

Berta/w1|Will people ask for help sooner?|I hope so. Trust will need rebuilding along with everything else.|Will you help Wren?|When she asks. She is quite capable of deciding what help she needs.|What would ordinary care look like?|People coming before a small problem has become an emergency.
Della/s0|Did he ever thank Maelis?|Not openly. That disappointed me more than his earlier mistake.|Why did he fear her before?|He repeated stories without asking the person they described.

Della/s1|Did the mint spread that quickly?|Once established, it sent growth where I had planted other things.|Is it easier to manage in a pot?|Yes, provided I keep an eye on it. The pot is a boundary, not a promise.
Della/e0|Does mint grow over the pot?|It can trail and root where it touches soil. I keep it apart from the beds.|Could you cut it back?|Yes. A smaller plant is easier to keep where I intended.
Della/e1|Have you spoken to her yourself?|Yes. That is why I prefer questions to rumours.|What should I ask her?|About the help or goods you actually need. She can answer for herself.

Della/w0|Why do people blame Maelis?|Fear makes a convenient story easier to repeat than a difficult question about authority.|Has she asked you to defend her?|No. I can stop spreading nonsense without needing instructions.|What has she done for neighbours?|Offered help when people were willing to ask her directly.

Della/w1|Will the rumours stop now?|Not by themselves. People must stop treating repetition as evidence.|What can you do about them?|Ask who actually witnessed the thing being claimed.|Do you think everyone will change their mind?|No. I can still insist on honesty when I hear a claim repeated.
Ewan/s0|Was the face drawn by a witness?|I do not know. It records one reader's anger, not the whole town's opinion.|Could a note mislead you too?|Of course. It adds a perspective, not a verdict.

Ewan/s1|Where would you find those accounts?|Household records, letters, and people whose families remember the work.|Would anyone read that history?|People might recognise their own lives in it. That is a reason to try.

Ewan/e0|Can household accounts be wrong?|Yes. I would compare several and ask what each one leaves out.|What could the two pages disagree about?|A proclamation might promise plenty while a household records rising food costs.

Ewan/e1|What if the stain hides words?|Then it is a real loss. I can value a well-read book and still ask people to protect it.|Do you eat while reading?|Not over a borrowed book. Admiring evidence of use is no excuse for carelessness.

Ewan/w0|How do you spot that bias?|Watch whom the writer credits, whom they blame, and what they never mention.|Does it make every fact false?|No. It makes the account incomplete and self-serving.|Where can you check the claims?|Other accounts from the time, particularly ones written for purposes other than praising him.

Ewan/w1|Why keep the proclamations?|They show what people were told, alongside evidence of what actually happened.|Could our side exaggerate too?|Certainly. Winning does not make every account accurate.|Who should write the new history?|More than one person, with their sources available for others to question.

Fara/s0|Was your mother upset about the jug?|Yes. The ornament did not undo the accident, but she appreciated the care that went into it.|Did Sela use every fragment?|Only pieces suitable for the ornament. Broken glass does not all become safe decoration.

Fara/s1|Do you ever refuse a broken thing?|Yes, when I cannot use it safely or have no space left.|How do you choose what to keep?|Whether I can name a likely use, instead of merely hoping one will occur.

Fara/e0|How do you store sharp pieces?|Wrapped and separated, where nobody will mistake them for harmless scraps.|Does sorting give you ideas?|Sometimes. Other times it tells me I should have kept less.

Fara/e1|Does your mother like the ornament?|She does. It catches light in a way the old jug never did.|Do you still regret breaking the jug?|Yes. Finding a use for the pieces did not make breaking it a favor.

Fara/w0|Do royal orders delay local repairs?|Skilled hands can only do so much at once. Grand orders tend to move to the front.|Why do broken windows matter so much?|They let weather into an ordinary home. Beauty is not the only purpose glass serves.|Can scraps help with repairs?|Sometimes, if they suit the job. Not every leftover is sound enough.

Fara/w1|Will you help repair homes?|Where I have something useful to offer. Sela understands work I would not attempt.|Can everything be mended with scraps?|No. Some work needs new material, and pretending otherwise wastes time.|What would you repair first?|Things keeping the weather out, before ornaments for rooms already comfortable.

Garrick/s0|Did you ever meet the apprentice?|Eventually. I told them I had heard the improvement before seeing it.|Why notice one hammer among so many?|A repeated pause catches the ear when you hear it every day.

Garrick/s1|Why did the forges close?|There was too little work to keep both running through that winter.|Did people leave town?|Some sought work elsewhere. The quiet meant more than a pleasant afternoon.

Garrick/e0|Do you still hear mistakes?|Of course. The difference is that the rhythm no longer stops in the same place.|Will you tell the apprentice?|I have. They seemed relieved that someone noticed the good part too.

Garrick/e1|Do all the workshops stop together?|Not exactly. Enough stop around midday that the change is noticeable.|Do you take lunch then too?|Usually. It is easier to enjoy it without talking over a hammer.

Garrick/w0|Does more work help the town?|When it pays fairly and leaves people able to live. Exhaustion is not prosperity.|Why does tiredness hurt apprentices?|They make mistakes and remember less. Craft needs attention, not merely hours.|Can the workshops refuse orders?|A royal order carries consequences an ordinary customer cannot threaten.

Garrick/w1|What would a normal shift mean?|Time to work carefully, then enough rest to return fit for the next day.|Will the apprentices learn faster?|With less exhaustion, they stand a better chance.|Could shorter shifts hurt wages?|That needs discussing honestly. Workers should not pay for the change by going hungry.

Hester/s0|Did she explain before cutting it?|No, which I objected to. She explained after I stopped staring at the hole.|Could you mend it straight away?|With her help. I was glad to learn before needing that skill in bad weather.

Hester/s1|Is a crooked knot still reliable?|This one holds properly. Appearance is less important than how the strain runs through it.|Did the boy learn anything useful?|How to tie it, and why I would not help trap his sister behind a door.
Hester/e0|Can you reuse badly tangled cord?|If it remains sound after untangling. Frayed cord needs replacing.|Does that take longer?|Less time than discovering a weak knot when the net is loaded.

Hester/e1|How do you choose the size of the spaces?|For the intended catch and the cord. Too wide or too close causes different problems.|Can a stretched net be repaired?|Sometimes. I check the sound mesh before deciding how much to replace.

Hester/h|Why would rivals help each other?|An overdue boat might carry somebody's family. Competition can wait.|What happened after the boat returned?|Relief, repairs, and eventually the old arguments about catches.

Hester/w0|Do you pay tax before repairing the net?|The crown expects its share whether repairs are due or not.|What happens if you cannot replace it?|The next catch suffers, and the household has less to spare again.|Could a collector understand that?|If they listened to the people doing the work, perhaps.

Hester/w1|Have your neighbours begun learning?|We have agreed to practise with sound cord before tackling a damaged net.|Why teach rather than repair it yourself?|They need to manage when I am not there.|Will you stop helping once they learn?|No. Having another skilled pair of hands helps everyone.

Junia/s0|How long have you been saving?|Long enough to know the cost of a replacement pair of socks rather well.|Why choose a lamp?|It is something I will enjoy each evening, not just on special occasions.

Junia/s1|Will amber glass brighten the room?|It will color the light near my chair. I am not expecting it to imitate a whole sunset.|Why that chair?|It is where I sit at the end of the day. That is where I want the change.

Junia/e0|Do you write the amount down?|Yes. Counting again does not add a copper, however encouraging I hope it will be.|What if another expense comes first?|Then the lamp waits. The fund belongs to me, not the other way around.
Junia/e1|Have you seen one lit?|Yes, which was more persuasive than seeing it on a shelf.|Would another color do?|Perhaps, but amber is the one I keep thinking about.

Junia/w0|Has the levy delayed your lamp?|Yes. I can wait; someone who needs food has a more urgent loss.|Do neighbours help with bread?|Where they can. Their own cupboards are being counted too.|Why does the crown keep raising it?|The explanation changes. The effect on a small purse does not.

Junia/w1|Will you finally buy the lamp?|When I have enough. I would enjoy buying it without guilt about wanting something pleasant.|What would you want for your neighbours?|Enough security that a small pleasure is an ordinary choice.|Does comfort matter after so much trouble?|Yes. People deserve more than surviving until the next demand.

Kellan/s0|Did you find the fault?|Damp had affected the mechanism. Taking it apart exceeded my talent for putting it back.|Would you let someone repair it?|A skilled repairer, gladly. I have proved what my own inspection can accomplish.

Kellan/s1|Does everyone eat at the same time?|Not everyone, but enough workshops quieten that the difference carries through the street.|Do you miss the noise at midday?|No. I know why it has stopped, and I enjoy my meal.

Kellan/e0|Do you still have all the parts?|I kept them together. That is the most successful part of the repair so far.|Why not ask a clockmaker?|I should. Admitting defeat took longer than dismantling the clock.

Kellan/e1|Did the clock make you late often?|I blamed it often. Leaving late was my own contribution.|How do you keep appointments now?|I allow more time instead of trusting a faulty mechanism to rescue me.

Kellan/w0|Why does their timing bother you?|They interrupt working people and act as though collecting payment is the only business in town.|Can you ask them to wait?|I can ask. They are less interested in my schedule than their own.|Do levies arrive regularly?|Regularly enough to expect one, unpredictably enough to make planning awkward.

Kellan/w1|What would you like to remember this year for?|People beginning work they chose, and celebrations they could afford.|Will you keep track of the difficult years?|Yes. I simply want the good events to occupy more of the page.|Will the town's rhythm change?|If people can rest and celebrate more, I hope so.

Lysa/s0|What made the crooked bird appealing?|Its tilted head looked curious. The perfect one seemed less like a creature to me.|Where did you put it?|At home, where the light reaches it. I do not carry fragile glass on errands.
Lysa/s1|Why carve birds?|A twig already suggests a shape sometimes. I enjoy trying to find it.|Would your family buy one?|They have plenty. I may need customers with emptier shelves.
Lysa/e0|What improved the beak?|Looking at the whole shape before cutting away too much.|Will you keep this one?|For now. It will be useful to compare with the next attempt.

Lysa/e1|Does the flaw weaken the glass?|It is a misshapen ornament, not cracked glass. I still handle it carefully.|Would you choose it again?|Yes. I wanted something I liked looking at, not a judge's approval.

Lysa/w0|How can he mistake fear for admiration?|Nobody dares explain the difference to him, and he prefers the flattering answer.|Can people hide their fear?|Sometimes. A practiced smile is not necessarily a happy one.|Would you tell him directly?|I would be frightened. That is exactly the problem with demanding admiration.

Lysa/w1|Have you chosen a glass dragon?|Not yet. I like being able to consider one openly.|Why would it have needed courage?|People watched for anything that seemed to praise dragons beyond the king's control.|Where would you put it?|At home, in the light. An ornament should be allowed to be an ornament.

Cinder/s0|Was it difficult to keep the ember alive?|It needed suitable protection and care. Grandmother had years of practice.|Why share a flame between houses?|It helped neighbours whose hearth had gone cold start their morning fire.
Cinder/s1|Who chose your name?|My family remembered that winter and what kept us warm through it.|Do you like answering to it?|Mostly. The confusion around a hearth provides regular entertainment.

Cinder/e0|Were you nervous carrying it?|Yes. I had watched it done before attempting the short journey myself.|Was the neighbour grateful?|Very. Their cold hearth mattered more than the small size of my gift.

Cinder/e1|What do you enjoy watching?|The changing light and the way wood settles as it burns.|Do you tend it all evening?|I check it as needed. Watching a fire and leaving it unattended are different things.

Cinder/w0|Why could they not afford fuel?|Other demands had taken what little money they had set aside.|Could the crown help them?|It could take less or provide help. Instead, neighbours fill the gap.|Can a shared coal solve that shortage?|Only the difficulty of starting a fire. They still need fuel to keep warm.

Cinder/w1|Will people still need that help?|Yes. A change in rule does not instantly mend a cold house.|Who taught you to offer it?|Grandmother. She knew whose hearth had gone out before they asked.|What else would help the neighbours?|Enough fuel and sound homes. A kindness should not be the whole winter plan.

Warden/s0|Was the wheel difficult to repair?|It needed proper attention, not another hurried splash of oil.|Do you still know when he is near?|Sometimes by the cart, sometimes only when the door opens. Supper survives the uncertainty.

Warden/s1|Does he tell you what he likes?|He tries to say anything will do. An empty wrapping is more informative.|Do you pack something for yourself too?|I should remember to. He is not the only person doing a day's work.

Warden/e0|Was he pleased to fix it?|Very. He had heard that squeak all the way home, not just from the next lane.|Do you miss worrying less about his return?|I still know when he should be home. I just cannot expect a wheel to report for him.
Warden/e1|What travels well in the pack?|An apple or a little cheese, properly wrapped.|Does he ever share the extra?|I expect so. I pack enough to allow for his generosity.

Warden/w0|Why are the carts late?|Long shifts, heavy loads, worn equipment. Demanding speed does not mend any of those.|Does he get time to rest?|Not enough when another royal order is due.|Have you told the officials?|They hear a complaint where I am describing a person's health.

Warden/w1|Was it a shorter shift?|Short enough that he could eat and talk before falling asleep.|What did you talk about?|Things outside the work. It was good to remember we had those.|What should change next?|Reasonable hours people can rely on, instead of one lucky evening.
Ember/s0|How did you discover the dust was yours?|I took off my coat and saw what fell from it near the fresh bread.|Did you apologise?|Yes. Less promptly than I should have, which he remembers.
Ember/s1|Where did the pebble come from?|A walk when I had time to notice something besides work.|Do you ever take the things out?|Of course. Keeping them clean is meant to let me enjoy them.

Ember/e0|What do you keep under the cloth?|A cup, a pebble, a ribbon. Small things I want to see without coal dust over them.|Does covering them help?|Enough. I would rather lift a cloth than wash everything again.

Ember/e1|Do you brush your coat before visiting?|Yes. I prefer paying for bread to providing its extra ingredient.|Were you embarrassed about the accusation?|Very. A clear apology was overdue by the time I managed it.

Ember/w0|Where does the mine's wealth go?|Much of it leaves in royal orders. The dust stays with the households doing the work.|Do workers receive a fair share?|Not enough to make the town's living conditions match the boasts.|What would a fairer share change?|Sound homes, better equipment, and less fear of an unexpected expense.

Ember/w1|How could workers have a say?|By being included when pay, hours and repairs are decided.|What should the earnings improve first?|The conditions people live and work in, before another fine entrance somewhere else.|Will speaking up be easy?|No. We have had practice being ignored, and officials have had practice ignoring us.

Dagna/s0|Why open the window after cleaning?|The room was hot and close. Dust was not the only thing we had to live with.|Did you clean it all again next day?|The necessary parts. I stopped treating every speck as an emergency.
Dagna/s1|Which task can safely wait?|Polishing. Food and dangerous clutter are different matters.|Would a set stopping time help?|Probably more than choosing an impressive amount of unfinished work.

Dagna/e0|Was it any harder the next morning?|No. That was inconvenient evidence against my worrying.|What did you do with the evening?|Sat down, and tried to notice something besides the unpolished surface.
Dagna/e1|Can you close the window during dusty work?|Sometimes. I choose a better time to air the room when I can.|Do the voices cheer you up?|Usually. It is pleasant to hear life beyond the chores.

Dagna/w0|Does mine dust reach every room?|Enough of them that cleaning feels like a second shift.|Who notices that work?|The people doing it. Official accounts rarely count a household's cleaning hours.|What would reduce it?|Better conditions around the work and the streets, not another instruction to scrub harder.

Dagna/w1|What would cleaner water change?|Washing, cooking, the ordinary work of a household. It would matter every day.|Why shorter shifts?|People need time and strength left for their families and homes.|Are you expecting quick results?|I want honest plans and visible work, rather than another banner doing the promising.

Lode/s0|Can a rhythm really tell you everyone is safe?|Not reliably. It is familiar noise, and that comforts me; it is not a report from the workshop.|Does the forge still wake you?|A sudden change can. Familiar noise is easier to sleep through.
Lode/s1|Was the cup in danger of falling?|It could work toward the edge. The cloth stopped it moving around.|Why keep it near the forge wall?|It suits the room. We found a safer way to keep it there.

Lode/e0|Would you rather the forge were quiet?|When a shift has ended normally, yes. Unexpected silence is what catches my attention.|Do you check every time it stops?|No. Listening through a wall does not make me the foreman.
Lode/e1|Did the cloth stop the rattle?|Yes, and the cup no longer creeps along the shelf.|Why protect that particular cup?|It was a wedding gift. Replacing it would not replace the memory.

Lode/w0|What were workers promised?|That one more push would bring easier times. The push kept growing instead.|Could they refuse the longer shift?|Not without risking income they needed.|Why no longer believe the promise?|Because the extra work happened immediately, while the promised improvement kept moving away.

Lode/w1|How could a quiet forge mean rest?|With planned shifts and enough paid work to support people without exhausting them.|Do you worry about closures?|Yes. I remember that silence can mean a lost livelihood too.|What would reassure you?|Clear arrangements workers can depend on, not guesses about tomorrow's work.

Pike/s0|Why would the miner hide being hungry?|Pride, embarrassment, fear of looking unprepared. Any would make a first shift harder.|Does your husband still share?|When someone needs it. I have made his pack a little more forgiving.

Pike/s1|Why leave the carts behind?|I want a meal whose pauses are not filled by work passing the door.|Would your husband come?|That is the plan. A picnic together, with no one expected underground afterwards.

Pike/e0|Does a separate wrapping help?|It makes the extra portion easy to hand over without sharing half-eaten food.|Do you always pack more now?|When supplies allow. I cannot feed a whole crew from one basket.

Pike/e1|What would make a good spot?|Dry ground, a little shelter, and enough quiet to hear the person beside me.|Is planning half the enjoyment?|At the moment. I should eventually let the picnic happen too.

Pike/w0|Why are crews kept below so late?|Another order takes precedence over the agreed finish.|Can food last through those shifts?|Not always. That is why I add what I can.|Does the crown pay for the extra provisions?|Not to the households packing them.

Pike/w1|Will knowing the finish time help?|It means supper can be supper, rather than waiting with it going cold.|What if work is delayed honestly?|Delays happen. I want people informed and cared for, not kept below without a thought.|What would you do with a free evening?|Eat together and finish a conversation before either of us falls asleep.

Hallow/s0|Could the frame be damaged too?|Yes. Replacing screws alone is pointless if the wood no longer holds them.|Have you shown anyone the old screws?|When discussing repairs. Evidence is more useful than simply raising my voice.

Hallow/s1|Could you fix her spectacles?|With her explaining what she could not see. That was one of my first useful jobs.|Did she mind asking for help?|Less than I expected. She wanted working spectacles, not an audience for her pride.
Hallow/e0|Does the label include the dates?|Yes. Otherwise it is merely a jar of screws and an argument.|Why not throw them away after the repair?|I want a record if the damage keeps recurring.

Hallow/e1|Can the noise mislead you?|Yes. A squeak can come from a different part than the one you first suspect.|What if it works when you check?|Ask what happens when it fails. Conditions and weight can change the problem.

Hallow/w0|Do the blasts damage houses?|They can shake loose fittings. Repeated repairs cost time and materials.|Have you asked for the costs to be covered?|Yes. The answer is usually about whose responsibility it supposedly is.|Why keep repairing them yourself?|The window must close whether anyone accepts the bill or not.

Hallow/w1|Which repairs should the mine help pay for?|Damage linked to its work, assessed honestly.|Will the screws prove the cause?|They record repairs. I also need dates and other evidence; a jar alone proves little.|What would stop the argument recurring?|Clear responsibility for inspecting damage and paying for necessary repairs.

Quarrel/s0|Do you actually like his bread?|Enough to return for twenty years. Do not let him add that to the price.|Does he enjoy the argument?|He saves his best answers for me. I would call that evidence.
Quarrel/s1|Have you tried sleeping farther away?|Yes. Flint's snoring has an impressive reach.|Does Flint listen to your complaints?|More than he admits. He can usually tell which one needs a hammer.

Quarrel/e0|Was the step on your property?|It was one I could reasonably repair. I checked before taking a hammer to someone else's work.|Did complaining help at all?|It identified the problem. The hammer supplied the missing part.

Quarrel/e1|Do you ever compliment the bread?|He would worry if I stopped after mentioning the crust was excellent.|Would you shop somewhere else?|If the bread failed. The argument alone would not keep me fed.

Quarrel/w0|Are people afraid for you?|Some are. I take that seriously even when I dislike lowering my voice.|Would a complaint change his mind?|Perhaps not. Silence certainly lets him pretend there is none.|What should people be allowed to question?|Decisions affecting their food, work and safety, without punishment for asking.

Quarrel/w1|Has Flint asked you to quiet down?|He has made suggestions. I am exercising my newly comfortable right to consider them.|What will you complain about now?|Repairs and prices. I never lacked material.|Will you listen to complaints about yourself?|Reluctantly, which is apparently still progress.
Flint/s0|Did the traveller stay long?|One evening. The lesson stayed considerably longer.|Have you taught others?|When they ask about tending a hearth. It is useful knowledge to share carefully.

Flint/s1|Does she help after pointing things out?|Yes. She would prefer the complaint to become unnecessary.|Do her complaints ever tire you?|Certainly. I can be tired and still admit the step needs repairing.
Flint/e0|Does it save starting from nothing?|That is the benefit when the hearth has been tended properly.|Who taught you to do it?|A traveller we gave supper to. It was an excellent exchange.

Flint/e1|How do you tell a serious complaint?|I ask what needs changing. There is usually a practical answer underneath.|Does she know you listen that way?|I think so. She brings me the jobs she wants done.

Flint/w0|Have you already cut every expense?|Enough that another demand takes something necessary, not merely convenient.|Why does saving no longer help?|There is a limit to what a household can spare. The crown behaves as though there is not.|Do neighbours share fuel?|When they can, but everyone's stores are under pressure.

Flint/w1|How did Quarrel choose the list?|She knows which neighbours have been short, and asks instead of guessing.|Will sharing leave you enough?|We will count our own needs first. Creating another cold household would not help.|Does she complain while helping?|Usually. The wood arrives all the same.

Winnie/s0|Was Nan a good dancer?|Very. She could follow a tune that left the rest of us counting our feet.|What happened with the fiddle?|Ask her. I would rather you heard her version with that particular smile.

Winnie/s1|Did you plant the flowers?|When they still had roots worth saving. Not every enthusiastic gift survived.|Did she like spring best?|She liked the first signs of it. A small flower could become the day's news.
Winnie/e0|What made Mum laugh?|Her own mistakes, often before admitting what had happened.|Did you always forgive her?|We still dealt with the trouble. A laugh simply made being cross harder.

Winnie/e1|Does she listen as much as she talks?|Yes. She leaves with my news as faithfully as she brings her own.|Do you bring her things too?|Of course. Friendship need not keep an exact account to go both ways.

Winnie/w0|Were gatherings safer before?|We had quarrels, but a complaint did not always begin with checking who could hear.|Do you still invite neighbours?|Yes, though people choose their words more carefully than they should need to.|What ordinary thing do you miss most?|A conversation that stays on its subject instead of turning into a warning.

Winnie/w1|Would Nan really dance again?|Ask her. I suspect she will deny being ready while remembering every step.|Who would play the music?|Someone who knows the tunes we keep humming anyway.|Would you dance too?|If my feet agree. I intend to make them a persuasive offer.

Ned/s0|What warning does damaged leather give?|Cracks, thinning and stretched holes. You have to look before trusting it under strain.|Can you repair every break?|No. Sometimes a replacement is the safer and more honest answer.
Ned/s1|Why wouldn't Dad take payment?|He said I needed a hand, not an invoice.|Does Nan know why you help?|Yes. She reminds me friendship is not a debt that must never be paid off.

Ned/e0|Should a worn strap be replaced at once?|It depends on the damage and what it carries. I inspect it before deciding.|What makes a repair unsafe?|Unsound leather around the stitching. A neat stitch cannot strengthen material already failing.

Ned/e1|Who needed your help afterwards?|Neighbours with repairs or heavy work. Your father had not limited the favor to one person.|Did helping someone else settle it?|It stopped me thinking only in terms of repayment.

Ned/w0|Did you hurry the repair?|I worked promptly, but would not skip checking the damaged leather.|Did the officer understand?|He understood that a broken strap would delay him more than my inspection.|Could his horse have been hurt?|A failed fitting can endanger horse and rider. Rank does not change that.

Ned/w1|Will you work differently now?|The stitching still needs the same care. I hope people will argue less about the time it takes.|What if a customer insists on speed?|I explain the risk and refuse an unsafe shortcut.|Do experienced riders listen?|Usually. They know a failed fitting is not worth saving a few minutes.

Nan Ferrow/s0|Can you teach me one of her songs?|When you are home awhile, love. I still remember the tunes better than every verse.|What did Dad usually find?|Whatever she had just put somewhere sensible and then forgotten.

Nan Ferrow/s1|Did anyone help you look after me?|Neighbours helped with errands and meals. I did not have to manage every hour alone.|Was I a difficult baby?|You had opinions about being put down. I was rather glad somebody wanted holding.

Nan Ferrow/e0|How did you get the boots so muddy?|You had found a puddle you considered worth investigating very thoroughly.|Did I help clean the laundry?|As much as a small boy could. Mostly you helped me discover where else the mud had gone.

Nan Ferrow/e1|Do you miss having me underfoot?|I miss you, love. The extra space has not entirely made up for it.|What if I forget where things belong?|Then you can ask. Familiar does not have to mean being tested at the door.

Nan Ferrow/h|What news did visitors bring?|Who had married, what the market cost, whether the road was passable.|Did travellers always stay the night?|If there was room and they needed it. Supper did not come with a rule either way.

Nan Ferrow/w0|Did you worry I would repeat something?|Yes. A child should not have to understand why an ordinary complaint is dangerous.|Were you always frightened of him?|Not every minute. That is how such things settle in: you begin treating caution as normal.|What do you want for me?|To speak and live without organising every choice around his temper.
